entry.title: Main :: RE: Ports created by [AI]
entry.dc:creator: Aranya
entry.dc:subject: Main
entry.content:
Author: Aranya
Posted: Fri Oct 30, 2026 8:07 am (GMT 0)

In my opinion, although I'm neither an AI user nor someone who has ever done any programming, I can only see objections coming from a section of the community which, in my view, doesn't seem to have taken very well to the "democratisation" of access to creating content for the console.

I understand the desire to make a distinction and clearly identify which projects are AI-assisted and which aren't, since the effort involved and the merit are completely different. That's only fair. However, being opposed to everything made with AI seems absurd to me, as long as it doesn't affect people's jobs, steal other people's work, or cause anyone any harm.

I have nothing against an AI-enhanced Mortal Kombat, but I would be absolutely against an AI-generated Razing Core 2 made without Badcomputer's permission.

Furthermore, I believe that providing feedback on AI-assisted creations can encourage their creators to refine and develop their work further, rather than immediately jumping into a new project just to get likes or attract attention.

entry.title: Main :: RE: Ports created by [AI]
entry.dc:creator: baude
entry.dc:subject: Main
entry.content:
Author: baude
Posted: Fri Oct 30, 2026 8:05 am (GMT 0)

My take.

In my line of work (I’m an analyst programmer), I use AI—increasingly so. Anyone who uses AI beyond a casual, superficial level knows that we neither should nor can assume the final result will be what we want unless we put in the necessary effort ourselves. Ultimately, the people who produce great work today with the help of AI are the very same people who were producing great work yesterday, without it.

I agree that, lately, this forum has seen too many submissions of projects created almost entirely (or perhaps entirely) using AI, where the quality reflects a near-total lack of human effort. The individuals behind these low-quality games likely wouldn't have been able to create a game at all—or, if they had, it would have been of equally poor quality.

On the other hand, there have also been several recent submissions of games generated—partially or entirely—with AI that are of exceptionally high quality. I won’t name names; I think we’re all familiar with such examples. The creators behind these projects clearly know what they’re doing; they approach their work with care, attention to detail, and genuine effort. Is there a difference compared to those who build everything from scratch, the "artisanal" way? Obviously, yes: they have a machine to assist them in their efforts. But... so what?

No, really—that’s my conclusion: so what?

I don’t want to miss out on these extraordinary projects from talented people who happen to use AI as a tool. And with this sort of anti-AI sentiment that seems to be taking root, I get the feeling that we’re already starting to lose some of them.

I think a dedicated subforum for AI-assisted projects would be a good idea. I don’t see it as a "ghetto" or a form of segregation; rather, I believe those of us who truly understand that AI, quality, and hard work are not mutually exclusive—and I suspect we are the majority—will continue to engage with that subforum with the same enthusiasm we bring to this great forum.

entry.dc:creator: Guy
entry.dc:subject: Main
entry.content:
Author: Guy
Posted: Fri Oct 30, 2026 7:32 am (GMT 0)

If the sole purpose of a dedicated sub-forum is to quarantine all AI users regardless of their specific projects, how they use the technology or their participation in the rest of the forum by hiding them away or removing them from search indexes then I am not in favor of it.

I created homebrew content before the advent of AI, now I use it in my projects : it’s a useful tool and everyone responsibility to use it (or not use it) in line with its underlying philosophy.

I understand that enthusiasts who invest their passion, time, work and teaming to doing everything by hand hold a certain vision of homebrewing are losing visibility. That's unfair.

So in my view, it makes more sense to give greater visibility to those who choose to develop everything from scratch.

But I would rather see AI banned here than end up with two communities that don’t speak to each other.

entry.title: Competitions :: RE: Competitions 2027 - 30th Anniversary!
entry.dc:creator: Maxim
entry.dc:subject: Competitions
entry.content:
Author: Maxim
Posted: Fri Oct 30, 2026 1:54 am (GMT 0)

I think it is impossible to define a percentage scale that people can agree on. Some people are easily triggered by AI cover art, for example, even if the rest is created traditionally. That seems like it’s <10% to me. On the other hand, if 10% of the code was “vibed” that seems like a lot to me. And that’s still assuming I can make an accurate measure of that percentage.

By making the boundary vague I hope that means people will err on the side of caution. I’m hoping the “AI disclosure” requirement will ensure people give a clear picture of how much it was used and that can help provide some examples for us to set clearer boundaries in future.

One thing I’d like to rule out - at least for the next competition - is an AI-positive category.

- Too much AI. ("Too much" is up to the whims of the SMS Power! elves and cannot be defined.)

We may want to clarify this a little better before the competition happens, but in the current climate the general intention is that an entry where e.g. ~10% of the work is aided by AI would likely be accepted (e.g. an additional language, selected artwork), but an entry where ~50% of the work is done by AI wouldn't. This is not a firm rule here, but sort of aim to provide a general background intent about this.
